title: Mbakhal, Fishermen’s Rice with Nététou
author: Amina Savoura
desc: Rice cooked in a tiof-head broth with two fingers of liquid over it, and a ball of pounded nététou buried in the rice, cooked 20 minutes, then crumbled on top.
longDesc: Afrik’s mbakhal is a fishermen’s rice where the seasoning goes in twice. A tiof head and a piece of dried fish boil in salted water; 25 g of nététou is pounded with a chile and the onion and stirred in. The fish come out and the rice cooks in the broth — with ‘two fingers of liquid’ standing above it at the start. The remaining nététou is pounded with the second chile and salt, shaped into a ball, buried in a well in the rice, and removed after 20 minutes, to be crumbled over the finished plate. Indigenous butter or palm oil is drizzled on top.
ingredients: 125 g nététou (a possible misprint against 1 kg of rice — reported as printed)
1 tiof head, or 600 g fresh fish
100 g indigenous butter (liquid or clarified butter), a high-fat butter
steps: Put the tiof head and the dried fish in a pot of cold salted water. Bring to a boil.
Pound 25 g of nététou with a chile and the onion. Reduce to a paste and stir it into the boiling pot.
Take out the fish and keep it warm. Add the rice to the sauce — there should remain two fingers of liquid over the rice at the start; if not, add a little hot water.
Pound the rest of the nététou with the second chile and salt and form it into a ball. Make a small hole in the centre of the rice, put the ball in, cover and continue cooking.
After 20 minutes, remove the ball and set it aside.
Eat the fish with the rice, crumbling the cooked nététou mixture over the top.
Drizzle everything with indigenous butter or palm oil.
chefTips: Two fingers of liquid above the rice at the start is the printed measure — it replaces a water quantity and is easy to check.
The nététou ball is a vessel for the seasoning: it steams in the rice, then is crumbled over as a condiment.
Nététou is bought here. Taste it before adding salt; it is already salty.
If 125 g of nététou looks like too much for 1 kg of rice, it is the page’s own figure — start with less and keep the ball.
commonMistakes: Leaving the rice too dry at the start.
Burying the ball and forgetting to take it out.
Over-salting before the nététou is in.
reheating: Steam gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Whole-fish broth gives protein and minerals.
Fermented locust bean (nététou) is a concentrated protein and fat source.
culturalNote: The Afrik introduction, read by the second pass only, describes mbakhal as a dish of hand-rolled millet couscous with a peanut sauce — then the page prints a rice recipe. The page contradicts itself; both are recorded. It also says the dish is Wolof, a lunchtime dish shared from a communal bowl, and less famous than thiéboudiène or yassa.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Mbakhal des pêcheurs Lébous du Sénégal’. Byline: ‘Amina Savoura’. Publication: Afrik. Date as printed: ‘Publié le 7 septembre 2012 à 16h46, mis à jour le 10 avril 2026 à 11h33’. Yield: none printed (6 is an editorial estimate). TWO-PASS; quantities agree.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION IN THE SOURCE, recorded not resolved: the introduction (read by pass two only) describes millet couscous steamed under a peanut sauce; the ingredient list says ‘1 kg de riz’. The introduction also names ‘poisson séché (guedj)’ though guedj appears nowhere in the list.
SUSPECTED MISPRINT, as printed: ‘125 grs de nététou’ against 1 kg of rice is a very large quantity.
The Lébou attribution in the title could not be supported: no source in this collection attributes any dish to the Lébou ethnic group; the title is the page’s own.

THE CUE, a short fragment: ‘il faut qu’il reste deux doigts de liquide’ — printed with a typo, ‘en début e cuisson’. The ball is removed ‘au bout de 20 minutes’. Prep and cook times in this entry are estimates; only the 20-minute stage is printed.
Nététou is bought in this recipe; no fermentation is performed and no fermentation claim is made. Yeet and kecc do not appear.
